content_voiceover: This slide is titled Bernard-Soulier Syndrome misdiagnosed as ITP, and the peripheral smear illustrates exactly why that mistake happens so often. Multiple arrows point to giant platelets, several approaching the size of the surrounding red cells or even small lymphocytes, set against a background of thrombocytopenia, findings that superficially resemble ITP on a quick smear glance. Bernard-Soulier Syndrome is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex, the receptor that binds von Willebrand factor to initiate platelet adhesion, so unlike ITP it is not immune mediated, and it will not respond to steroids or IVIG. The key laboratory clue is absent ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation that is not corrected by adding normal plasma, which distinguishes it from von Willebrand disease, where mixing with normal plasma restores the response. Flow cytometry showing absent or markedly reduced CD42b, the GPIb marker, confirms the diagnosis. Boards love this pairing, giant platelets plus thrombocytopenia should always prompt review before labeling a patient with ITP.
keypoints: BSS classically mimics ITP: thrombocytopenia + giant platelets on smear
Deficient GPIb-IX-V complex - the VWF receptor
Absent ristocetin aggregation, NOT corrected by normal plasma (vs VWD)
Flow cytometry: absent/reduced CD42b (GPIb) confirms diagnosis
keypoint_voiceover: Bernard-Soulier Syndrome is a classic ITP mimic because it also causes thrombocytopenia, but the smear shows giant platelets that should trigger suspicion. It's caused by loss of the GPIb-IX-V receptor for von Willebrand factor, so ristocetin-induced aggregation is absent and, critically, is not corrected by adding normal plasma, unlike von Willebrand disease. Flow cytometry showing low CD42b confirms it, and since it isn't immune mediated, steroids and IVIG won't help.
